description:
This review of the EVGA (NVIDIA) RTX 3050 video card offers benchmarks vs. the RTX 3060, RX 6500 XT, GTX 970 & 1070 in 2022, and many more. We test gaming and power results.
Sponsor: Arctic Liquid Freezer II 280 (Amazon) https://geni.us/RJBy and Arctic MX-5 Thermal Paste (Amazon) - https://geni.us/EXf0I

NVIDIA's RTX 3050 launched today, but the EVGA RTX 3050 XC we're reviewing is actually *$80* more expensive than we were told to expect. That's because EVGA accidentally shipped it with the VBIOS for a higher-tier card, although the ultimate difference between the two is about 2-3%. The EVGA RTX 3050s are either $250 or $330 MSRP, although other cards, like the ASUS ROG Strix RTX 3050, go up as high as $500 MSRP (before even getting scalped). The range is massive. We're benchmarking the RTX 3050 in gaming, helping establish whether it's worth it to upgrade from a GTX 960, GTX 970, GTX 980 Ti (no), GTX 1070, or other cards.

The best way to support our work is through our store: https://store.gamersnexus.net/

comments.text:
I think that everyone gives this card an unfair bad shake. The only thing that is really bad about it is the lack of AV1 decoding. The rest doesn't matter to most people. The narrow memory bus just means that it isn't useful for mining at all. it is only decent at gaming. With inflation $200->$300 and this is being offered under $300 and it is actually in stock. Performance is like an RX580 which is the "top end card" from "2" generations ago. Sure it only has 4GB VRAM but this also means it cannot be used for mining ETH. 

So overall if you want to play games and you don't have a card then this does much better than any IGP solution and better than anything else under $300. Considering that even a 1650 Super is selling for $350-400 right now.... I expect that the RTX3050 won't be less than $400 in another week or less.... Whereas the 6500XT can actually be purchased. Does that make it great? No. 
Does it make it an option? Definitely. Especially for people on a budget.

But if you can get a 3050 at good price, get it, so you have a RTX gpu thinking on the future when you upgrade your cpu, and also you will enjoy it now with games that don't make an intensive use of cpu (the majority of games need powerful graphic cards but don't need powerful cpus so a quad core like yours can be enough for many games).

comments.text: @TitanSP  ok thank you for the advice. Do you still think that even with the bottleneck, the 3050 would perform better with the i5-4570 than the gtx 1650?
comments.author: @chunk9165

comments.text:
@chunk9165  Yes, 3050 will perform better in many games even with your cpu. Let's see an example of a new AAA game: God Of War. The recommended requirements for playing at 1080p and 60 FPS are:

- CPU: 4 cores at 3.5GHz. (Your cpu has 4 cores and can reach 3.6GHz when running on turbo mode).
- GPU: GTX 1070 8GB. (similar to 3050 8GB).

In this case, your cpu won't bottleneck your system. It's on the limit for the 1080p60 standard. But if you use it with a GTX 1650, the gpu will bottleneck your system. 

Many games have similar requirements, they can run nicely with 4 cores CPUs, but need powerful graphic cards for good framerates, and 8GB of video memory (to display hi-res textures).

In a few other games that are cpu-demandants, your cpu will not be enough, so it will bottleneck your system and the 3050 will not perform as good as it can. For example GTA V is a cpu-demandant game, I see my cpu at 50% usage (6 cores/12 threads at 4GHz), while in most games it's running at 20%.

I hope this help you to understand how bottlenecking works in games, and that the 19% cpu bottleneck I saw, can be 1% in many situations.

Maybe it's not a good idea to buy a gtx 1650 and being gpu-bottlenecked in many new games by a new graphic card...
comments.author: @TitanSP

comments.text: @chunk9165  Also I have to say if you have only 8 GB RAM on your system, it won't be enough for many recent games, because they use more than 10 GB RAM (God Of War, Cyberpunk...) I mean, can be enough, but it will limit the performance your cpu and gpu could get.

comments.text:
So close, with a mention that inflation is a thing that exists, but still missed it.  Really wish before completely ragging on the value GN especially, and Tech reviews in general would actually account for inflation and more importantly, the 25% tariff on GPUs.  While real world prices are crazy and sky high for all the reasons everyone discusses, there doesn't seem to be anyone even taking note of the fact that between inflation and the GPU tariff, the same money today on MSRP only buys you about 75% of 2017 dollars worth of GPU.  For example the $200 6500xt would be a $150 msrp in 2017 adjusted GPU dollars, and this $330 rtx3050 card would have had to  retail at $250 to net the board partners and GPU manufactures the same profit.  It is just disingenuous to blast the companies for raising the price when the United States decided to lower the value of it's dollar on world markets and impose protectionist tariffs that do nothing but raise the price to consumers.  
There are other factors such as increased manufacturing and fab costs that also go in to the mix, but that is more tied to the current shortages and such.  the tariff, on the other hand, won't go anywhere until consumers let their representatives know they won't stand for protectionist propaganda that hurts their standard of living while doing all  of nothing to move manufacturing out of China, just passing the added cost on to the consumers.

@sqlevolicious  high school econ class does not explain what's currently happening. And prices increase not only from printing money. Moreover, there were operations targeted at reducing amount of money, up to 1.9 trillion usd a day, did not help the inflation though.

Currently logistical problems mean that factories that previously were only assembly lines with ingredients coming in and product coming out might get one of components delayed, and that means stopping all production until it's delivered, and also they now need some place to store other ingredients. In warehouses they don't have. Managed by people they didn't need before. Even "better" if some ingredients have a restriction on storage conditions and might not function if stored improperly.
Delays are propagating over the whole system, so no one knows what their product will cost by the time it's delivered, and production costs already went up, so they know end price is going to rise by, say, 20-40%. And if they guess wrong and up their price by 20%, but price rose not by 20% but by 40 their capitalisation might suffer as they made an unprofitable decision, so everyone grabs as much as possible.
Also risk of damaging components means chance for more failed units in the very end, so everyone is insuring themselves to not suffer from damages. Which also increases cost of operation.

I would like to add to this point, by including a Dollar per Performance Value ($/PV) Chart in your testbenches to show just how screwed up the market is for current GPU launches at MSRP compared old GPU launches at MSRP. Here's what I mean:

I've been seeing a lot of peeps ask for a "Performance per Dollar" Comparison Chart, and honestly, I think this is the wrong way to go about doing that. What you don't want to do is take the Performance Values, or PVs, such as FPS (Highs, Mids, Lows) and/or various Production Benchmarks, and divide it from the base MSRP to get your "PV per Dollar Spent". Sure, it is good to see how many PVs you are getting per dollar our of the chip or gpu, but the problem lies in that there are multiple different PVs, and certain chips and gpus may only excel in specific PVs. To solve this, you would instead reverse that entire process to get the "Dollar Amount per PV". This would allow you to properly denote the strengths and weaknesses of a chip or gpu, since it gives you the dollar amount spent to get that additional specific PV.

In Gaming:
142fps(mid)/$349.99=0.405f/$
$349.99/142fps(mid)=$2.46/frame
In Production:
830pts/$349.99=2.371pts/$
18.6min/$349.99=0.053min/$
$349.99/830pts=$0.42/pt
$349.99/18.6min=$18.82/min

As you can see, the "Dollar Amount per PV" is much more concise and clearer to understand than "PV per Dollar Spent". As such, I definitely would love to see you guys instead make a "Dollars per [Performance Value]" Comparison Chart, as it would be much easier to convey how much value chips have at MSRP, and would be essential to viewers deciding on which chips or gpus to get based on their budget (not that you guys are doing a wonderful job on that already).

But yeah, just thought I'd throw my two cents in.

comments.text:
@Josh-cw8by   Scalping is BS no matter how you try to justify it. Global Pandemic, droughts in Taiwan, TSMC having production issues, all of these things help factor in to scarcity of the product. But scalpers botting a site to buy all the available product is not entrepreneurship no matter how hard you squint. 

Here's an example: I go to every store that sells groceries and buy the entire stock of every store within a 50 mile radius of my house. I then open my own store and sell all the groceries I bought, but at 3x MSRP. No one is forced to buy my groceries, they are free to go 50 miles away and buy food or to shop online and order food, or have no groceries and just eat out somewhere. (This is different than prices going up due to inflation, which you describe as the cause for increased pricing)

But what I am doing is not providing a service to those around me, I am assuming no part of the risk of the production or the logistics that result in the product being produced and shipped to the store. I am also providing no employment of my own, as the store is run by myself, and so the only person to benefit from this late stage is me. I am price gouging. It is that simple.  (Again, NOT the same thing as Inflation. )

Miners don't care if they are being gouged or not. When ETH is at $4700 miners feel bold about the potential ROI of GPUs, price inflated or not. At it's peak even a 3090 had a relatively short ROI even with an MSRP of $3000. But with ETH sitting at $25xx, much longer ROI, much less interest from miners. Plus Bitcoin relies on ASIC miners, as well as several other cryptos. (And with ASIC miners costing $12,000++ and bitcoin in the toilet I would imagine demand is down for those as well)

Depending on how many more countries continue to pass legislation outright banning proof of work cryptos from being mined within their borders, both Crypto prices and mining demand will continue to decrease. Following each ban of crypto mining there has been a temporary influx of additional stock (and a large dip in the value of Crypto). While some operations continue to chase cheap electricity, more are selling out. 

Market demand influences market pricing. When crypto continues to be banned, when mining sees increased crackdowns, if ETH 2 comes out and changes the way ETH is mined making ETH mining with a GPU useless, when chains become more difficult and require more computational power than a GPU farm can provide, when GPU manufacturers introduce hardware locks to prevent crypto mining,  when scalpers realize the mining crowd is gone and hobbyist aren't willing to pay their prices and they end up sitting on their stock for months, then prices will change. 

Its just like the SSD crytpo that came out, everyone wanted to mine with a harddrive. So the prices of SSDs skyrocketed for a short period of time. But then people realized it was stupid, and they stopped doing it, prices adjusted to meet demand. 

The same thing will eventually happen with Crypto mining on anything less than an industrial scale with industrial equipment. It wont be profitable any other way and it wont be sustainable any other way so only those with the means to own powerplants will continue to mine. 

Just like with DDR5 prices now. You want to know what I did instead of paying a scalper $800 for ram? I bought a DDR4 board and reused my old ram. I will upgrade if the price drops, if it doesn't, oh well, I still have a functioning computer. 

In conclusion, no, I don't think I will get used to it. You speak suspiciously like a scalper yourself.

comments.text:
@joseph1150  Yes. I agree with you, Scalpers do not have a monopoly on the market. But the economy does not function in a vacuum. And so the cause of low supply and high cost can be attributed to multiple factors. Not only is demand high. But it is high from a larger size of the population than it was 10-15 years ago. At one point it was enthusiast and hobbyist buying GPUs (outside of computational modeling cards like the Quadro series). Now in addition to hobbyist and enthusiast(which has itself grown), there is a small, but demanding subset of the population who desired large amounts of cards in order to facilitate mining. Over the past two years, as stated previously, the world underwent and continues to undergo a pandemic, which causes labor shortages, which causes production shortages and shipping delays. Ports slowed down, shipping cost went up. Ports could not offload. TSMC couldn't produce. As a result Nvidia could not produce the cards required to meet demand. Scalpers saw an opportunity to make a quick buck, and took it. Where available they bought up possible stock and became resellers. This is not to say that scalpers have caused Nvidia to increase the cost of the product at MSRP. Production cost and profit margins made Nvidia increase the cost of the GPUs. 

What this does mean though is that scalpers caused the overall cost for the consumer to increase over MSRP.  You can call this discovery if you wish, but a 3090 selling for $3000 on Amazon or eBay or Newegg is gouging. The scalper incurred zero cost for the production of the product and suffered zero losses for any product that was out of stock. 

Are scalpers responsible for Nvidia setting the base price of the 3050 at $250? No, that is Nvidia's decision. 

But are scalpers responsible for a 3090 selling for $3000 on Amazon/Newegg/eBay? Absolutely. 

And since scalpers had acquired some percentage of the stock allocated for the entire market then they influenced the overall market price for that GPU, by a relevant percentage. Not the MSRP, but the real market price. 

However all of this fails to take into account mining and its influence on the market and what happens to the market after its influence lessens. That remains to be seen. If potential profit is not there for miners then cards will stop being purchased at $3000 a pop because its not profitable to do so from any perspective. If demand decreases then the price will follow it. Once a single person stops needing to acquire 120 GPUs at once this will change demand. Once demand lessens and production ramps up it will become unprofitable for scalpers to operate in this sphere.

 This means GPUs will once again sell for MSRP or something that closely resembles it. This DOES NOT mean that Nvidia will lower the MSRP, as again, this is decided by production factors. But it does mean less $3000 3090s and more $1500 3090s.

comments.text:
Completely agree, but some counterpoints:
-Not all slots are made equal - using a full length slot will mean users are most likely to install in the slot the motherboard manufacturer intended for the GPU, which may be lower latency/have better built power delivery
-the full length slot will provide better structural support for the card, so less GPU sag
-mid length PCI-E slots seem to be less common on boards these days anyway, so this use case is less likely that it might have been historically
-Possible economies of scale/experience of board partners with this physical slot make it cheaper to manufacture cards with the full length connector than retooling for something else
-More people would be aware of the reduced number of links if the connector is physically different - if you don't read a review you might not notice

But yes, they probably should use a shorter PCI-E connector on those cards, it'd only open up potential use cases, as fringe as they are.
